text:
If you've been told that you have high 
cholesterol, you're not alone. It's

something that affects millions of Americans. 
There are many different risk factors that

contribute to high cholesterol. Some of them 
you can't control and others you can control.

According to the American Heart Association, 
start with these key lifestyle habits.

Eat a heart-healthy diet. Enjoy fruits, 
vegetables, whole grains, beans, nuts,

seeds, and lean proteins such 
as poultry and fish. Limit

ultraprocessed foods that are high in 
saturated fats, added sugar, and sodium.

Get moving. Physical activity is a great 
way to increase your HDL, the good stuff,

which helps to decrease your LDL, the 
bad stuff. Whether you're swimming,

walking your dog, or riding your bike, getting 
aerobic exercise on a regular basis is a great

way to keep your cholesterol in check. Manage 
weight. Achieving and maintaining a healthy

weight has many benefits. Being overweight or 
obese tends to raise your LDL and lower your HDL.

Avoid tobacco products. If you're a smoker, 
stop smoking. If you have high cholesterol

and you smoke, you're at an even higher risk for 
heart disease than non-smokers. Kicking the habit

may not only improve your cholesterol, but it 
will reduce your risk for many other dangerous

diseases. Get 7 to 9 hours per day of restful 
sleep. Poor or irregular sleep has been linked

with lower HDL and higher LDL and triglycerides. 
Establishing a consistent sleep routine,

and creating a relaxing environment can support 
your body's ability to regulate cholesterol.

Unfortunately, there are some people who can't 
control their cholesterol just by making healthy

lifestyle changes. There are a variety of 
reasons why, and among them is something

known as familial hypercholesterolemia or FH. 
That's just a fancy way of saying that a person's

high cholesterol runs in their family. which 
is why it's always a good idea to know about

your family's cholesterol history. But there's 
great news for people who can't control their

cholesterol through lifestyle changes alone. 
Cholesterol lowering medication have been

proven to be safe and effective in controlling 
cholesterol. If you need cholesterol medication,

your health care provider can design a 
treatment plan that's right for you. By

taking control of your own health, you're not only 
improving your long-term cardiovascular health,

but it also comes with some fantastic side 
effects like feeling good and living a longer,

healthier life. Get started now by 
visiting heart.org/cholesterol.
